title: Community Partnership that Can Influence a Decision
before: Explore how DSD staff describe open choices honestly, support usable participation, and return a truthful account of community influence.

turns.text: This discussion opens Community Partnership that Can Influence a Decision. It’s about inviting community knowledge into services, policy, learning, or relationships at DSD, and being honest about what that knowledge can actually change. The course begins with an invitation that sounds generous: staff ask people to “design together” a service introduction.

Except the service route and explanation are already settled. The only thing that can still change is the photograph. That doesn’t make the meeting useless, and a limited invitation can still be worthwhile. The problem is the description. When we call a reaction to a settled choice “shared design,” we promise an influence people won’t find when they arrive.

So the course separates kinds of participation. Informing, asking for advice, and developing an approach together each offer a different kind of influence. A clear invitation names the question, what can change, and who holds the actual decision responsibility. Sometimes that means saying plainly that an eligibility rule, for example, is outside this discussion.

Timing matters too. If a problem is framed only around administrative speed, we may miss understanding, usable support, or the burden of repeated contact. Inviting affected perspectives while the problem can still be examined means their knowledge may change the question itself, not just our preferred answer. Welcoming people doesn’t give everyone identical authority, but it should make the decision role visible.

Practical conditions shape whose input arrives, too. Materials, communication support, preparation time, and scheduling all affect who can contribute. An open invitation isn’t the same as an available opportunity. The course is also careful about cost. Community expertise can take real effort, so staff make resource questions visible through approved arrangements rather than promising compensation or inventing a rate.

There’s a workplace version as well. New employees may be invited to comment on onboarding after the next version is already final. Their experience is heard, but it can’t affect that version. You’ll work through a practice situation like that and think about how to treat their knowledge seriously when the choice has already closed.

Another thread is what a contribution actually does. Someone might ask a question, name a concern, or offer an alternative. Participation doesn’t establish agreement with the proposal or permission to publish someone’s story. And when people disagree, the course asks us to compare their reasons against the same decision question instead of forcing several concerns into one community position.

Culture briefs have a helpful but limited role here. A brief can help you prepare questions about trust, meaning, or communication. It can’t assign a viewpoint based on someone’s identity or make one person the representative of a whole community. The course keeps room for different experiences within every community.

You’ll also practice with a quotation. A participant asks for a usable way to clarify a service notice, and staff publish the quote as evidence of community support. The question is what a better response would look like. Then there’s a rewrite activity: choose one open question and write an invitation that states what people can examine and how their contribution will be considered.

The close focuses on the return. A truthful account explains which contributions informed the change, which didn’t, and why, and what is still under consideration. It may include disagreement. It also respects people’s choice about future participation, so one contribution doesn’t quietly turn someone into the permanent voice of a community.

As you go, keep in mind a meeting, survey, or conversation where you asked others for input, or were asked yourself. What could actually change at that point, and was that clear to everyone? Bring that example along. The practice will help you describe an open choice honestly and carry community knowledge into decisions where it can make a difference.

guidance.title: Matching the invitation to the choice
guidance.text: Before inviting anyone, write the decision in one sentence and list what can still change. If only a small detail is open, describe that detail plainly. If a larger question should be open, raise it with the responsible roles before promising shared design. People can decide whether to contribute when the invitation tells them what their effort can influence.

guidance.title: Your next genuine opening
guidance.text: Think of a group or person whose knowledge has helped your work before. When is the next point where their input could still change something? Consider how you would explain that opening, the limits around it, and their freedom to decline. What would you want to hear before deciding whether to give your own time to someone else’s decision?
